title: Correlation Visualizer MicroSim
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Data Science
description: Set the correlation of a scatter plot, switch to curved patterns, and drag points to see how Pearson r, R squared, and Spearman rank correlation respond.

learningObjectives: Students will be able to compare Pearson and Spearman correlation across linear, curved, and outlier-affected scatter plots and explain what each number does and does not reveal about the relationship.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Comparison of contrasting cases with direct manipulation of data points
keyQuestions: Why can r be close to 0 when the points clearly follow a curve?
Why does one outlier change Pearson r more than Spearman ρ?
If r = 0.8, what fraction of the variance in y does the best-fit line account for?
commonMisconceptions: A correlation near 0 means the variables are unrelated (it only means there is no straight-line relationship).
r = 0.8 means 80% of the variance is explained (the share is r² = 0.64).
A strong correlation shows that x causes y (correlation alone cannot show causation).
The correlation tells you how steep the line is (r measures how closely the points follow a line, not its slope).
assessmentOpportunities: Students are shown three scatter plots (a tight falling line, a U shape, and a rising curve with one outlier). For each they decide whether Pearson r is positive, negative, or near zero, whether Spearman ρ would be noticeably different, and why.
